source_refs.note: Distillation Process, printed as 15.2.1 with Figures 15.6 and 15.7 and the Interesting Information box, pages 328-329.

blocks.text: Simple distillation separates the solvent from a solution. Take 100 cm3 of sea water and set up the apparatus as shown in the Figure 15.5, adding a few boiling chips to prevent bumping and making the apparatus air-tight so that no vapour escapes. Heat the flask gently with a Bunsen burner and let cold water circulate slowly around the condenser. Water (or alcohol) evaporates when its boiling point is reached, its vapour passes through the condenser, and the circulating water condenses it back to liquid: the distillate, collected in the receiving flask. The components left in the distillation flask are collectively the residue.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Figure 15.5 is the crystallization figure, not a distillation apparatus. The book prints no figure of the simple distillation set-up; Figure 15.7 shows the fractional distillation apparatus.

Separating two miscible liquids in this way is fractional distillation, successful only if the boiling points differ by about 25 degrees C. The distillation column, a glass column filled with glass beads to increase the surface area for condensing the vapour, separates the mixture into its components by boiling point (Figure 15.7).

blocks.alt: Graph of thermometer reading against time. The curve rises, stays flat at 78 degrees C where ethanol distils, rises again and levels off at 100 degrees C where water distils.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.6: Fractional distillation of ethanol / water mixture (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.6).

blocks.alt: Fractional distillation apparatus: a distilling flask heated by a flame, vapour rising through a fractionating column with a thermometer at the top, a water-cooled condenser with cold water entering at its lower end and leaving at its upper end, and the distillate collecting in a conical flask.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.7: Fractional distillation setup (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.7).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 15.7 shows cold water entering the condenser at its upper end and leaving at the lower end. Cold water enters at the lower end and leaves at the upper end, as drawn above, so that the jacket stays full.

When a mixture of ethyl alcohol and water is heated, the alcohol distils first because its boiling point, 78 degrees C, is lower than water's 100 degrees C; while the alcohol distils the thermometer stays at 78 degrees C. As soon as the temperature starts to rise above 78 degrees C the receiving flask is replaced with a new one; when the thermometer reaches 100 degrees C water boils and is collected after condensation as the second distillate, so both components are obtained pure (Figure 15.6). Natural petroleum is a mixture of many compounds used as fuels, such as petrol, diesel, kerosene and furnace oil, whose boiling points are not very different; they are separated as fractions by fractional distillation in a fractionating column.
